title: Wall Street falls into correction as Nasdaq drops 5% and Nvidia sinks 14% on SEC report
dek: The S&P 500 and Dow are now 10% below their peaks after the worst week for US shares since 2020. Bitcoin fell below $60,000. Indian shares, which hit a nine-month high on Friday, face a test on Monday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell into correction territory on Friday, closing more than 10 per cent below their record highs, as a sell-off in artificial-intelligence and chip shares deepened into the worst week for American stocks since the start of the pandemic in March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28 per cent in a single session and wiped out its gain for the year.

Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker, fell about 14 per cent to $125.53 after reports that enforcement staff at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are examining its accounting. Neither the SEC nor Nvidia has commented on the reported inquiry, and a civil investigation does not establish wrongdoing. The selling spread to bitcoin, which fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and to gold.

## What happened

The S&P 500 lost 3.7 per cent to close at 6,910.39. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261 points to 22,617.73, leaving it down 2.7 per cent for 2026. The Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93 per cent, to 48,147.33; it is less exposed to technology shares than the other two indices, according to reports. The Nasdaq-100, which tracks the largest technology companies, briefly fell more than 20 per cent below its recent high during the day, the usual definition of a bear market.

Over the week, the Dow lost about 8 per cent, its worst week since March 2020, the S&P 500 about 8.6 per cent and the Nasdaq about 10 per cent, its biggest weekly fall in more than six years, according to reports. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street's main gauge of expected swings, closed above 30 for the first time since March.

Chip shares took the heaviest losses. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell about 13 per cent, Broadcom between 12 and 14 per cent (reports differ) and Micron nearly 14 per cent. Shares of Asian chipmakers listed in New York also fell sharply: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's US shares lost about 9.5 per cent, and US-listed funds tracking Taiwan and South Korea fell about 11 per cent and 8 per cent respectively, pointing to a difficult open for those markets on Monday.

Anthropic, the AI company that listed on the Nasdaq on Thursday, fell 8.5 per cent to $88.91 on its second day of trading, giving back about half of its first-day gain but staying above its $83 offer price.

Investors moved into safer assets. Shares of Walmart, Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble rose about 1 per cent each, and US government bond prices rose, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield down to about 4.99 per cent, according to reports. Bitcoin fell more than 4 per cent to about $59,500 and ether about 6 per cent to roughly $1,650. Gold futures fell nearly 4 per cent, reports said. Brent crude, by contrast, rose 0.6 per cent to $92.57 a barrel.

## The Nvidia questions

The latest blow to Nvidia was a report on Friday that SEC enforcement staff are looking at the company's books. It is not known when the inquiry began or which financial statements or transactions are being examined, according to reports. Earlier in the week, reports said the SEC was investigating whether Nvidia's disclosures to investors, particularly those relating to Asia, had been misleading.

The company has been under unusual pressure since Jensen Huang, its co-founder, resigned as chief executive on 12 November amid concerns in Washington over a Singapore-based customer that US investigators suspect of diverting restricted chips to China. Nvidia reported on 17 November that its quarterly revenue had more than doubled to $115.8 billion, but said the filing of its full quarterly report would be delayed while an independent committee of its board carries out a review, according to reports. Mr Huang and the company's general counsel are due to be interviewed behind closed doors by three House of Representatives committees in early December.

Nvidia shares have now fallen for seven weeks in a row, their longest losing run since the 2008 financial crisis, according to reports.

## Background

The sell-off reflects growing doubts over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars that technology companies are spending on data centres for AI will earn an adequate return. "The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts," Richard Saperstein of Treasury Partners said, according to reports. Strategists at BNP Paribas described Friday's moves as panic selling, while Deutsche Bank called the market "very oversold", reports said.

Interest rates are adding to the pressure. US bond yields are close to 5 per cent, and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said this week that waiting longer to raise rates risked falling behind the curve, according to reports.

Friday's fall followed a 2.2 per cent drop in the Dow on Thursday, which took it below 50,000 for the first time since June, on the day Anthropic made its market debut.

## What it means for India

Indian shares have so far moved in the opposite direction. The Sensex rose 897.96 points to 83,919.71 on Friday and the Nifty 286.30 points to 25,800.60, both at their highest in about nine months, with analysts saying that global investors were moving money out of AI and chip shares in Taiwan and South Korea and into markets such as India, which have few such companies. The rupee closed at about 92.67 to the dollar, its strongest in about seven months, according to reports.

The question for Monday is whether that rotation holds after Friday night's losses in New York. Indian information technology companies earn much of their revenue from US clients, and a sharp fall in American shares can weigh on them. A weaker dollar and lower US bond yields, on the other hand, tend to help emerging-market currencies such as the rupee. Indian markets will be closed on Tuesday, 24 November, for Guru Nanak Jayanti, according to reports, so next week has only four trading sessions.

For Indian retail investors in cryptocurrencies, bitcoin's fall below $60,000 extends losses for the year.

## Key numbers

- S&P 500: 6,910.39, down 3.7% on the day and about 8.6% on the week
- Nasdaq Composite: 22,617.73, down 5.28%; down 2.7% for 2026
- Dow Jones: 48,147.33, down 949.73 points (1.93%); down about 8% on the week
- Nvidia: $125.53, down about 14%
- Anthropic: $88.91, down 8.5% (offer price $83)
- Bitcoin: about $59,500, down more than 4%
- Brent crude: $92.57 a barrel, up 0.6%
- Sensex (Friday close): 83,919.71, up 897.96 points

## What happens next

Asian markets open on Monday morning, India time, with Taiwan, South Korea and Japan likely to feel Friday's chip losses first. In the United States, the week is shortened by the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, 26 November. Investors will watch for any statement from Nvidia or the SEC about the reported inquiry, and for the congressional interviews of Nvidia's former chief executive and general counsel in early December.
